title: Where Is the HVAC Filter Located?
h1: Where Is the HVAC Filter Located in Your Home?
description: Your HVAC filter is usually behind a return air grille or in a slot at the furnace or air handler. Here is where to look in garages, closets and attics.
quick_answer: Most HVAC filters are in one of two places: behind a return air grille in a ceiling or wall, or in a slot or cabinet right at the furnace or air handler. In Southern California homes, check the hallway ceiling first, then the garage, a hall closet or the attic where the equipment sits.
body:
Every forced-air system has a filter somewhere on the return side, before the air reaches the blower. The trick is that installers put it wherever the layout made sense, so two homes on the same street can have filters in completely different spots.

Here's how to find yours, starting with the most likely places.

Is the filter behind a return air grille?

In many San Diego and Orange County homes, the filter sits behind a large return grille. Look for one in the hallway ceiling, a hallway wall, or near the center of the house. It's usually the biggest grille in the home.

A filter grille often has one or two latches or thumb screws on one edge and hinges on the other. Open it and the filter slides out. If the grille is screwed shut on all sides and there's no filter behind it, the filter is probably at the equipment instead.

Some homes have more than one filter grille, one for each return. If you have two or three large grilles, check each one.

Where is the filter at the furnace or air handler?

If there's no filter at the grille, go to the equipment. In our area, furnaces and air handlers are usually in one of these spots:

  • Garage. Often in a closet or on a raised platform along a wall.
  • Hall or interior closet. Common in condos and older single-story homes.
  • Attic. Very common in tract homes. The unit usually lies on its side.

Once you find the unit, look for the filter in these places:

  1. A thin slot with a removable cover where the return duct meets the furnace.
  2. A thicker filter cabinet, sometimes 4 to 5 inches deep, between the return duct and the furnace. This is often called a media filter.
  3. Inside the lower blower door on some upflow furnaces.
  4. A filter rack at the bottom of the air handler on a platform.

Before opening any panel on the furnace itself, turn the system off at the thermostat. If the filter is behind the blower door, turn off the switch at the unit as well. Don't take apart anything that's held on with wiring or gas connections.

What if the system is in the attic?

Attic furnaces almost always have the filter at a ceiling return grille below, so you don't have to climb up there every month. If you can't find one, the filter may be at the unit itself.

If you do go into the attic, step only on the joists or a walkway, bring a light and avoid hot summer afternoons. Attics in inland areas can get extremely hot. If the climb isn't easy or safe, have a technician show you where it is during your next tune-up.

How do I know what size filter I need?

The size is printed on the edge of the old filter, such as 20 x 25 x 1. The first two numbers are the width and height, and the last is the thickness. Buy the same size and thickness.

If there's no old filter, measure the opening, not the grille face. Write the size on the inside of the grille or on the furnace cabinet so you don't have to hunt for it next time.

A filter that's too small leaves gaps around the edges. Air takes the easy path around it, and dust goes straight to the coil and ducts.

Which way does the filter go in?

Look for the arrow on the frame. It points in the direction the air flows, toward the furnace or air handler and away from the room. At a ceiling grille, that means the arrow points up into the ceiling.

How often should I change it?

For a basic 1-inch filter, checking every month and changing every one to three months is a good starting point. Thicker media filters usually last longer. Pets, construction, wildfire smoke, Santa Ana winds and running the fan all day mean you'll be changing it more often.

The simplest rule: if it looks gray and dusty, change it. If you're not sure your filter is the right type for your system or you'd like an upgrade, our indoor air quality team can help you pick one that fits.
faqs: Can an HVAC system have more than one filter?

Yes. Homes with several return grilles may have a filter in each one. Some systems also have a filter at both the grille and the furnace, which is usually unnecessary and can choke airflow. Pick one location and use the right filter there.
What if I can’t find my HVAC filter at all?

Check every large grille, the garage, closets and the attic around the equipment. Some systems were installed without a filter slot at all, which lets dust coat the coil. A technician can find it or add a proper filter rack.

Yes. Ductless mini-split indoor units have washable mesh filters behind the front cover. Lift the cover, slide them out, rinse them with water, let them dry fully and put them back. Check them about once a month during heavy use.
Is it safe to run the system without a filter?

Only for a few minutes while you swap filters. Running without one lets dust coat the blower and AC coil, which cuts efficiency and can lead to frozen coils and costly cleaning. Keep a spare filter on hand.
